{{Short description|Special setting of hypothesis testing}}

In [[statistics]], '''universal hypothesis testing''' is a special case of binary [[Statistical hypothesis test|simple hypothesis testing]]. The universal problem is to distinguish between a simple null hypothesis <math>H_0: Q = P</math>, and the most general composite alternative <math>H_1: Q \neq P</math>, using [[Independent and identically distributed random variables|independent and identically distributed]] samples from <math>Q</math>. The setting is sometimes referred to as [[goodness of fit]] testing, or one-sample testing. 

A simple binary hypothesis testing problem involves distinguishing between <math>H_0: Q = P_0</math> and <math>H_1: Q = P_1</math>, using samples <math>X_1, \dots, X_n \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} Q</math>. In the traditional setting of hypothesis testing <math>P_0, P_1</math> are known apriori. A composite version of this problem involves sets of probability distributions <math>\Omega_0, \Omega_1</math>, and asks to distinguish between <math>H_0: Q \in \Omega_0</math> and <math>H_1: Q \in \Omega_1</math>. In contrast, the universal setting corresponds to the special case of composite hypothesis testing, where the null hypothesis is simple, <math>\Omega_0 = P</math> and the alternative hypothesis is the set of all distributions other than <math>P</math>, <math>\Omega_1 = \{F: F \neq P\}</math>. For example, someone might want to know if a particular coin was fair, i.e. <math>\mathbb{P}[X = H] = \frac{1}{2} = \mathbb{P}[X = T]</math> or not, i.e. <math>\mathbb{P}[X = H] \neq \mathbb{P}[X=T]</math>, where <math>H,T</math> denote the coin coming up heads or tails. 

The [[Error exponents in hypothesis testing|asymptotics]] of universal hypothesis testing were first discussed in Hoeffding's work on optimal tests for multinomial distributions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hoeffding |first=Wassily |date=April 1965 |title=Asymptotically Optimal Tests for Multinomial Distributions |url=http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.aoms/1177700150 |journal=The Annals of Mathematical Statistics |volume=36 |issue=2 |pages=369–401 |doi=10.1214/aoms/1177700150 |issn=0003-4851|doi-access=free }}</ref> There have been many subsequent works on the topic<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Levitan |first=E. |last2=Merhav |first2=N. |date=August 2002 |title=A competitive Neyman-Pearson approach to universal hypothesis testing with applications |url=http://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/1019834/ |journal=IEEE Transactions on Information Theory |volume=48 |issue=8 |pages=2215–2229 |doi=10.1109/TIT.2002.800478 |issn=0018-9448|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Zeitouni |first=O. |last2=Gutman |first2=M. |date=March 1991 |title=On universal hypotheses testing via large deviations |url=http://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/75244/ |journal=IEEE Transactions on Information Theory |volume=37 |issue=2 |pages=285–290 |doi=10.1109/18.75244|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Li |first=Yun |last2=Nitinawarat |first2=Sirin |last3=Veeravalli |first3=Venugopal V. |date=July 2014 |title=Universal Outlier Hypothesis Testing |url=http://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/6799184/ |journal=IEEE Transactions on Information Theory |volume=60 |issue=7 |pages=4066–4082 |doi=10.1109/TIT.2014.2317691 |issn=0018-9448|url-access=subscription |arxiv=1302.4776 }}</ref> in many directions. While Hoeffding's initial results were restricted to distributions with finite supports, later results developed solutions for continuous distributions using extensions of the [[Kullback–Leibler divergence|Kullback-Leibler Divergence]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Yang |first=Pengfei |last2=Chen |first2=Biao |date=April 2019 |title=Robust Kullback-Leibler Divergence and Universal Hypothesis Testing for Continuous Distributions |url=https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8528471/ |journal=IEEE Transactions on Information Theory |volume=65 |issue=4 |pages=2360–2373 |doi=10.1109/TIT.2018.2879057 |issn=0018-9448|url-access=subscription |arxiv=1711.04238 }}</ref> or [[Kernel_embedding_of_distributions#Measuring_distance_between_distributions|kernel methods]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Zhu |first=Shengyu |last2=Chen |first2=Biao |last3=Chen |first3=Zhitang |last4=Yang |first4=Pengfei |date=April 2021 |title=Asymptotically Optimal One- and Two-Sample Testing With Kernels |url=https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/9354188/ |journal=IEEE Transactions on Information Theory |volume=67 |issue=4 |pages=2074–2092 |doi=10.1109/TIT.2021.3059267 |issn=0018-9448|url-access=subscription |arxiv=1908.10037 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Zhu |first=Shengyu |last2=Chen |first2=Biao |last3=Yang |first3=Pengfei |last4=Chen |first4=Zhitang |date=2019-04-11 |title=Universal Hypothesis Testing with Kernels: Asymptotically Optimal Tests for Goodness of Fit |url=https://proceedings.mlr.press/v89/zhu19b.html |journal=Proceedings of the Twenty-Second International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics |publisher=PMLR |pages=1544–1553 |arxiv=1802.07581}}</ref>
